Set Up LangGraph and LangSmith Studio on Windows: A Practical Guide

Prepare a Python environment in PowerShell, configure API keys, and connect LangSmith Studio to a local Module 1 graph.

By Victor Pereira · November 7, 2026 · Python / LangGraph

Part 1 · Windows setup and first Studio connection. This walkthrough ends with the Module 1 local development server running and its simple graph visible in LangSmith Studio. Executing the graph and exploring Modules 1–2 are future steps.

In this guideWhat is LangGraph?Two typical use casesOur learning path1. Get the course files2. Set up PowerShell3. Install Jupyter4. Set up LangSmith5. Set up OpenAI6. Set up Tavily7. Configure Studio8. Launch Module 1Official resources

What is LangGraph?

LangGraph is an open-source orchestration framework and runtime for building stateful AI agents. A workflow is represented as a graph: nodes perform work, edges determine the next step, and state carries information between steps. It combines ordinary Python logic with model calls and supports persistence, streaming, and human review. LangChain is optional. [1]

Two typical use cases

These illustrative applications use the capabilities described in the official documentation. [1]

01 · A support assistant

Keep conversation context, call a tool to look up an order, and use the result to answer a customer's question.

02 · A document review workflow

Analyze a document, draft a summary, and pause for a person's review before continuing.

Our learning path

This independent walkthrough accompanies LangChain Academy's Introduction to LangGraph — Python course. Today’s scope is environment setup through launching Studio with Module 1. Later installments will explore Module 1: Introduction and Module 2: State and Memory, using our own examples and execution notes. [2]

1. Get the course files

The official LangChain Academy GitHub repository contains the notebooks and module resources. Clone it with Git, or download the repository as a ZIP and extract it. Use either option; both provide the course files.

Terminal · clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain-academy.git
cd langchain-academy

If using the ZIP, open a terminal in the extracted langchain-academy-main folder instead.

Check the Python version

Terminal
python3 --version

2. Create and activate the environment in PowerShell

The course uses Unix-style shell commands, including source lc-academy-env/bin/activate. On Windows PowerShell, the activation script is in Scripts. Open PowerShell in the repository folder and run the following commands. These are the commands used in our lab; check the interpreter version before creating the environment.

Windows PowerShell · commands used in the lab
python3 -m venv lc-academy-env
ls
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope Process
.\lc-academy-env\Scripts\Activate.ps1

ls lets us check that the environment folder exists. The execution-policy command allows local scripts under RemoteSigned for the current PowerShell process; the change ends when that session closes. In our session, PowerShell requested confirmation and we entered Y. An organizational policy may override this setting. See Microsoft's execution-policy reference.

After activation, (lc-academy-env) appears at the start of the prompt. Python documents the Windows PowerShell activation path in its virtual environment guide.

Install the dependencies

With the intended environment active, install the repository requirements:

Windows PowerShell · install course dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

3. Install Jupyter

Follow the official Installing Jupyter guide. It provides pip instructions and also offers Homebrew as an option for macOS and Linux. For this Windows lab, use pip inside the activated lc-academy-env environment.

Windows package managers

Leading Homebrew alternatives for Windows include WinGet, Chocolatey, and Scoop. WinGet is Microsoft's official command-line package manager, included through the App Installer system component on Windows 11 and modern Windows 10 installations (Windows 10 version 1809 or later). If it is missing, install or update App Installer.

Check whether WinGet is available:

Windows PowerShell · check WinGet
winget --version

WinGet manages Windows applications; pip installs the Python packages used below. WinGet is not required for these Jupyter installation commands.

JupyterLab

A workspace for notebooks, files, and terminals. Install it, then launch it from the course repository folder:

Windows PowerShell · JupyterLab
pip install jupyterlab
jupyter lab

Jupyter Notebook

A notebook-focused interface for opening and running the course's .ipynb files:

Windows PowerShell · Jupyter Notebook
pip install notebook
jupyter notebook

Choose JupyterLab or Notebook to work through the course; both are listed here as options. Run each launch command separately. A running server keeps its terminal busy; press Ctrl+C and follow any confirmation prompt to stop it before continuing in that terminal.

Voilà (optional)

Voilà turns notebooks into interactive dashboards. It is optional for our introductory course work.

Windows PowerShell · Voilà
pip install voila
voila

Run voila from a folder containing notebooks to browse them, or target a specific file with voila your-notebook.ipynb.

Jupyter is included to prepare for the notebook lessons. Today’s demonstrated result is the Studio connection in section 8.

4. Sign up for LangSmith

LangSmith Observability helps inspect and debug an agent's execution through traces. Create an account at LangSmith, then follow the official account and API-key guide.

  1. Open Settings → API Keys → Create API Key.
  2. For this personal learning lab, choose Personal Access Token, enter a description such as langchain-academy, and select the intended default workspace and expiration.
  3. Create the key and copy it securely. The secret is displayed only once; use a placeholder in screenshots and published examples.

Create .env in the project root

In PowerShell, navigate to the repository root—the folder containing requirements.txt and lc-academy-env—then open the configuration file:

Windows PowerShell · repository root
notepad .env

Save the file as .env, not .env.txt. It belongs at the same folder level as lc-academy-env, outside the virtual environment directory.

File placement relative to the repository root
PathPurpose
.envLocal API-key and tracing configuration
requirements.txtCourse dependencies
lc-academy-env/Python virtual environment
module-1/, module-2/Course notebooks and resources

Add the following settings, replacing your-key locally:

.env · project-based course configuration
LANGSMITH_API_KEY="your-key"
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
LANGSMITH_PROJECT="langchain-academy"
# If you are on the EU instance, uncomment this line:
# LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT=https://eu.api.smith.langchain.com

Tracing variable: the supplied course notes use LANGSMITH_TRACING_V2=true. The current official SDK setup documents LANGSMITH_TRACING=true, which we use above. The project name follows this course's project-based workflow.

A .env file stores configuration; creating it does not automatically set variables in PowerShell or a notebook. The Python code must load it before initializing clients, for example with python-dotenv when installed:

Python · load the root .env from a Module 1 or Module 2 notebook
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv("../.env")

This relative path assumes the notebook's working directory is module-1 or module-2. If running from the repository root, use load_dotenv(".env"). Keep the actual .env out of Git and public uploads; only publish placeholders.

5. Set up an OpenAI API key

The course examples use OpenAI models. If you do not have an API account, start from the OpenAI API page or open the developer platform to sign up. Follow the official developer quickstart to create an API key.

Plan for API usage costs: do not assume a free API allowance. Check your account's billing and available credits before running the notebooks, and add funds or configure billing if required. Model requests are metered; review the current API pricing.

  1. In the developer platform, select your intended project and open API Keys → Create new secret key.
  2. Give the key a descriptive name, such as langgraph_labs_key, and review its project, expiration, and permissions.
  3. Create the key and store the secret locally. Do not include its value in screenshots, the article, or Git.

Add the key to the existing .env

From the repository root, run notepad .env again. Keep the LangSmith settings and append this line, replacing the placeholder locally:

.env · append to the existing configuration
OPENAI_API_KEY="your-openai-api-key"

As in the previous section, load the root .env into the notebook process before creating the model client. The SDK can then read OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment. Merely saving the file does not load it.

Using another model provider

You can adapt the exercises to another provider or a local model. Configure that provider's credentials when required, install its integration, and update the model name and invocation code. Check tool-calling support for agent exercises. Responses may differ from the course video—even with the same provider—so compare behavior and learning goals rather than exact wording.

6. Tavily for web search (optional for Modules 1–2)

Tavily provides web search and retrieval tools designed for AI agents and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Its search API gives an application access to current web sources that a model can use as context.

The course introduces Tavily in some Module 4 lessons, beyond today's setup and our planned Modules 1–2 follow-up. We record the setup here for later use. Tavily offers a free plan; check the current allowance and terms on signup instead of assuming the paid plans shown during onboarding are required.

  1. Sign up at tavily.com and obtain an API key from your account.
  2. Review the plan options. The supplied onboarding screen includes Continue on Free.
  3. Open the existing project-root configuration with notepad .env and append the following entry, keeping your LangSmith and OpenAI settings.
.env · append locally
TAVILY_API_KEY="your-tavily-api-key"

Load the .env file into the notebook process before using the search integration, as described in the LangSmith section. See the official Tavily documentation for API usage.

Example configuration — placeholders only:

.env · publication-safe example
LANGSMITH_API_KEY="your-langsmith-api-key"
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
LANGSMITH_PROJECT="langchain-academy"
# EU instance only:
# LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT=https://eu.api.smith.langchain.com
OPENAI_API_KEY="your-openai-api-key"
TAVILY_API_KEY="your-tavily-api-key"

7. Configure LangSmith Studio

LangSmith Studio, formerly LangGraph Studio, is a browser-based environment for inspecting and testing agents that expose the Agent Server API. It lets us explore a graph, interact with an agent, and inspect execution state alongside LangSmith traces. See the official Studio overview.

Studio can also help manage conversation threads and assistants, test prompts and datasets, inspect long-term memory, and revisit execution states through time travel. For this tutorial, our immediate goal is simply to connect Studio to a local course graph.

Prerequisites

  • A LangSmith account and API key.
  • The course dependencies and graph files.
  • The LangGraph CLI and a local Agent Server.

Local server prerequisites

The course stores Studio graphs in each module's studio folder. The local development server runs on your computer; the hosted Studio UI opens in your browser. The langgraph dev workflow does not require Docker.

Windows PowerShell · preparation, starting at repository root
# Keep lc-academy-env activated.
pip install "langgraph-cli[inmem]"
cd module-1\studio

# First-time setup only: copy the template if .env does not exist.
if (-not (Test-Path .env)) { Copy-Item .env.example .env }
notepad .env

# After saving the required credentials:
langgraph dev

Module-specific configuration: the supplied Module 1 langgraph.json points to ./.env. Therefore, configure module-1/studio/.env with the needed keys; the root .env used for notebooks does not automatically satisfy that path. Preserve the template's other settings, and use placeholders in published examples.

After a successful startup, the default addresses should be:

ServiceDefault address
Local Agent Serverhttp://127.0.0.1:2024
Studio UIOpen Studio connected to the local server
Local API documentationhttp://127.0.0.1:2024/docs

Keep the server terminal running while using Studio. Use the actual addresses printed by your server if they differ. Consult the local development guide for current CLI behavior.

Optional alternative: prepare multiple module .env files

For Module 1 alone, the manual configuration above is sufficient. The following adaptation is an alternative for preparing several modules; do not run it after manually editing module files unless you intend to replace them.

The course's Bash loop must be adapted for Windows PowerShell. Save the following as creating_env_by_module-powershell.ps1 in the repository root, beside requirements.txt:

creating_env_by_module-powershell.ps1 · author's adaptation
for ($i = 1; $i -le 5; $i++) {
    Copy-Item "module-$i\studio\.env.example" "module-$i\studio\.env" -Force
    Add-Content -Path "module-$i\studio\.env" -Value "OPENAI_API_KEY=""$env:OPENAI_API_KEY"""
}
Add-Content -Path "module-4\studio\.env" -Value "TAVILY_API_KEY=""$env:TAVILY_API_KEY"""

The loop copies the environment template for Modules 1–5, then appends the OpenAI key from the current PowerShell process. It also appends the Tavily key to Module 4. Although the course text mentions Modules 1–6, both its Bash example and this adaptation stop at 5; Module 6 is not processed.

Before running: -Force replaces existing module .env files with their templates. Back up any module-specific settings first. The script reads $env:OPENAI_API_KEY and $env:TAVILY_API_KEY; it does not read the repository-root .env. If these variables are unset in this PowerShell session, empty key values will be appended.

Check that the variables are present without displaying their values:

Windows PowerShell · presence check
if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($env:OPENAI_API_KEY)) {
    throw "OPENAI_API_KEY is not set in this PowerShell session."
}
if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($env:TAVILY_API_KEY)) {
    throw "TAVILY_API_KEY is not set in this PowerShell session."
}

Set or load those variables locally before continuing. Loading .env inside a notebook does not populate a separate PowerShell session. The copied templates must also contain the required LangSmith configuration; this script does not add the LangSmith key.

From the repository root, run:

Windows PowerShell · run the saved script
.\creating_env_by_module-powershell.ps1

If script execution is blocked, use the process-scoped policy step described earlier. Afterward, review the generated files locally, resolve any duplicate variable entries, and confirm their LangSmith and regional settings before starting Studio. Do not publish their secret values.

Evidence: the author supplied the PowerShell adaptation. The next section confirms the local server startup and Studio connection; the contents of the generated secret files are not published.

8. Launch Module 1 and open Studio

With the virtual environment active and the module configuration prepared, return to the repository root. Confirm the current location and list the files, then start the server from the Module 1 Studio folder:

Windows PowerShell · commands executed by the author
pwd
ls
cd module-1/studio
langgraph dev

pwd shows the current directory and ls lists its contents. In this PowerShell session, the forward-slash path module-1/studio works. The prompt retains (lc-academy-env), confirming that the virtual environment is active.

The supplied console output shows the local API at http://127.0.0.1:2024 and imports the simple_graph, router, and agent graphs. Open the printed Studio UI link while leaving the server running.

Today’s endpoint reached. The local Agent Server is running, Studio is connected to it, and the Module 1 simple_graph is visible. The graph has not yet been submitted for execution in the supplied screenshot. Model responses, LangSmith traces, Tavily search, and notebook execution are outside the results demonstrated here.

What runs locally? The development server and course graph code run on the Windows computer. The Studio interface is hosted at smith.langchain.com and connects to that local server. This is a development setup, not a production deployment or a fully local LangSmith installation.

Keep PowerShell open while using Studio. To finish the session, press Ctrl+C in the server terminal. Our next installment will move from setup to executing and understanding the graph, then state and memory.
